meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Remember, democracy never lasts long. It soon wastes, exhausts, and murders itself. There never was a democracy yet that did not commit suicide'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, John Adams wrote it, in a letter to John Taylor (dated 17 Dec 1814), printed in his Works, vol. 6 (1851), p. 484. Here is the line in full context.

source.excerpt: You say, I “might have exhibited millions of plebeians sacrificed to the pride, folly, and ambition of monarchy and aristocracy.” This is very true. And I might have exhibited as many millions of plebeians sacrificed by the pride, folly, and ambition of their fellow-plebeians and their own, in proportion to the extent and duration of their power. Remember, democracy never lasts long. It soon wastes, exhausts, and murders itself. There never was a democracy yet that did not commit suicide. It is in vain to say that democracy is less vain, less proud, less selfish, less ambitious, or less avaricious than aristocracy or monarchy. It is not true, in fact, and nowhere appears in history. Those passions are the same in all men, under all forms of simple government, and when unchecked, produce the same effects of fraud, violence, and cruelty.

author.bio: John Adams was a Massachusetts lawyer and revolutionary, and the second President of the United States (1797–1801). His Defence of the Constitutions of Government of the United States of America argued for balanced, mixed government against what he saw as the dangers of any unchecked single power, democracy included. In retirement he defended those views at length in letters like this one.

misattribution.heading: Right author, missing context
misattribution.intro: The attribution is correct. The problems are context and wording: the line is usually quoted on its own, as if Adams were dismissing democracy alone.

items.why: A few sentences earlier in the same letter, Adams writes: “I do not say that democracy has been more pernicious on the whole, and in the long run, than monarchy or aristocracy.” Right after the famous line, he says the same passions drive men “under all forms of simple government” (Wikiquote, XVIII, pp. 483–484 ↗). His target is any unchecked, single-power government.

The familiar punctuation follows the 1851 printed Works ↗. The Founders Online text quoted by Quote Investigator ↗ reads “Remember Democracy never lasts long. It soon wastes exhausts and murders itself. There never was a Democracy Yet, that did not commit suicide.” The words are the same.

items.who: “Democracy… while it lasts is more bloody than either aristocracy or monarchy”
items.why: Wikiquote notes that the sentence just before the famous line is “usually misquoted” in that form. In the letter it reads: “Democracy has never been and never can be so durable as aristocracy or monarchy; but while it lasts, it is more bloody than either” (Wikiquote ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: John Adams wrote it, in letter XVIII to John Taylor (dated 17 December 1814), printed in The Works of John Adams, vol. 6 (1851), p. 484 ↗. The same letter says democracy is no worse than monarchy or aristocracy.

context.heading: Why Adams wrote it
lead: In 1814 the Virginia senator John Taylor of Caroline published An Inquiry into the Principles and Policy of the Government of the United States, a long critique of the system Adams had set out in his Defence of the Constitutions (Wikipedia ↗). Adams answered in a series of letters. His grandson and editor, Charles Francis Adams, wrote that they “appear to have been sent to Mr. Taylor, as they were written” (Works, vol. 6, Editor’s Preface ↗).

In letter XVIII, Adams is answering Taylor’s charge that he had piled up victims of “democratic rage” to prove democracy worse than monarchy. Adams denies that and argues that pride, ambition and greed are the same under any simple government, and that only a balanced constitution checks them.
context.pull: Those passions are the same in all men, under all forms of simple government.
